concepts.title: SELECT: choosing columns
concepts.lede: A table is a grid of rows and named columns. `SELECT` picks which columns you want to see, and `FROM` says which table.

blocks.x: The tables below are a small support-desk database, like the tickets ReviewRadar classifies. Open the **Tables you can query** box in any exercise to see them.

SELECT name, country FROM customers;          -- two columns, every row

SELECT id, words AS length FROM tickets;      -- AS gives a column a new name

SELECT id, words / 200.0 AS minutes FROM tickets;   -- compute a value

x: `SELECT *` means every column. Handy for a quick look, but name your columns in real code.
Keywords are case-insensitive, but writing them in capitals makes queries easier to read.
`--` starts a comment. End a statement with `;`.

blocks.x: `/` between two whole numbers does integer division in SQLite and Postgres: `7 / 2` is 3. Use `7 / 2.0` to get 3.5.

blocks.q: Which query returns only the `plan` column of `customers`?
blocks.why: The pattern is `SELECT columns FROM table`.

exercises.prompt: Show every customer's `name` and `country`.
hints: You need two columns from one table.
List the columns after SELECT, separated by a comma.
`SELECT name, country FROM customers;`
exercises.solution: SELECT name, country FROM customers

exercises.prompt: Show each ticket's `id` and its `words` renamed to `length`.
hints: Two columns: `id` and `words`.
`AS` renames a column in the result.
`SELECT id, words AS length FROM tickets;`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, words AS length FROM tickets

exercises.prompt: For each ticket show its `id` and the reading time in minutes, named `minutes`, rounded to 2 decimals. Assume 200 words per minute.
hints: Divide `words` by 200.
Use `200.0` so the division keeps decimals.
`SELECT id, ROUND(words / 200.0, 2) AS minutes FROM tickets;`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, ROUND(words / 200.0, 2) AS minutes FROM tickets

concepts.title: WHERE: filtering rows
concepts.lede: `WHERE` keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition. Combine conditions with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`.

blocks.x: `NULL` means "unknown", so `x = NULL` is never true, even for NULL rows. Always write `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

blocks.q: Which clause correctly finds tickets that have not been resolved (`resolved_at` is missing)?
blocks.why: Only `IS NULL` tests for a missing value.

exercises.prompt: Find the `id` of every ticket that is `open` and has priority 3.
hints: Two conditions must both be true.
Text values go in single quotes: `'open'`.
`WHERE status = 'open' AND priority = 3`
exercises.solution: SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open' AND priority = 3

exercises.prompt: List the `name` of every customer who is not on the `free` plan.
hints: Use a comparison that means "not equal".
`<>` or `!=`, or `IN ('pro', 'enterprise')`.
`WHERE plan <> 'free'`
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE plan <> 'free'

exercises.prompt: Which tickets have no agent assigned? Show their `id`.
hints: The `agent_id` is missing (NULL) for these tickets.
`= NULL` never matches.
`WHERE agent_id IS NULL`
exercises.solution: SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE agent_id IS NULL

exercises.prompt: What does `SELECT id FROM tickets WHERE resolved_at = NULL;` return?
hints: Compare anything with NULL using `=`.
The result is not true, it is unknown.
`WHERE` keeps only rows where the condition is true.
exercises.why: `resolved_at = NULL` evaluates to NULL (unknown) for every row, and `WHERE` keeps only rows that are true. Use `IS NULL`.

concepts.title: ORDER BY, LIMIT and DISTINCT
concepts.lede: Rows come back in no guaranteed order unless you ask. `ORDER BY` sorts, `LIMIT` trims, and `DISTINCT` removes repeats.

blocks.x:
SELECT id, words FROM tickets ORDER BY words DESC LIMIT 3;     -- 3 longest
SELECT DISTINCT category FROM tickets ORDER BY category;       -- unique values
SELECT id FROM tickets ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC; -- tie-breaker after the comma

x: `ASC` is the default (smallest first); `DESC` is largest first.
Sort by several columns: later ones only matter when earlier ones tie.
`LIMIT n` keeps the first `n` rows, so it only makes sense after an `ORDER BY`.

blocks.x: Without `ORDER BY`, the database may return rows in any order and that order can change. Never rely on it.

blocks.q: Which gives the 5 most recent tickets?
blocks.why: Newest first means descending date, then take 5.

exercises.prompt: Show the `id` and `words` of the 3 longest tickets, longest first.
hints: Sort by length first.
`DESC` puts the biggest at the top.
`ORDER BY words DESC LIMIT 3`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, words FROM tickets ORDER BY words DESC LIMIT 3

exercises.prompt: List the distinct ticket categories in alphabetical order.
hints: You want each category once.
`DISTINCT` removes duplicates.
`SELECT DISTINCT category FROM tickets ORDER BY category`
exercises.solution: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM tickets ORDER BY category

exercises.prompt: List every ticket `id`, highest priority first. For tickets with the same priority, oldest `created_at` first.
hints: Sort by priority, then break ties.
Separate the sort keys with a comma.
`ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC`
exercises.solution: SELECT id FROM tickets ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC

concepts.title: Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG and GROUP BY
concepts.lede: Aggregate functions squeeze many rows into one number. `GROUP BY` does it once per group.

blocks.x: Press the buttons to group the rows by category and change the function.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets;                              -- how many rows
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM tickets GROUP BY category;
SELECT category, ROUND(AVG(words), 1) AS avg_words
FROM tickets
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;                                       -- filter groups

x: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs.
`WHERE` filters **rows before** grouping. `HAVING` filters **groups after** aggregating.
Every selected column must be either in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate.

blocks.x: You cannot use an aggregate in `WHERE`. `WHERE COUNT(*) > 3` is an error; use `HAVING COUNT(*) > 3`.

blocks.q: Which clause removes whole groups, such as categories with fewer than 3 tickets?
blocks.why: `HAVING` runs after grouping, so it can test aggregates.

exercises.prompt: How many tickets are in each category? Show `category` and the count as `n`.
hints: You need one row per category.
Count rows with `COUNT(*)`.
`SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM tickets GROUP BY category`
exercises.solution: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM tickets GROUP BY category

exercises.prompt: For categories with more than 3 tickets, show `category` and the average `words` rounded to 1 decimal as `avg_words`.
hints: Group by category, then keep only big groups.
Filter groups with `HAVING`, not `WHERE`.
`... GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 3`
exercises.solution: SELECT category, ROUND(AVG(words), 1) AS avg_words FROM tickets GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 3

exercises.prompt: How many **open** tickets are there for each priority? Show `priority` and `n`.
hints: Filter the rows before grouping.
`WHERE` comes before `GROUP BY`.
`WHERE status = 'open' GROUP BY priority`
exercises.solution: SELECT priority, COUNT(*) AS n FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open' GROUP BY priority

exercises.prompt: You want customers' ticket counts but only for customers with at least 3 tickets. Where does that condition go?
hints: The count only exists after grouping.
Aggregates cannot appear in `WHERE`.
`HAVING` filters groups.

explain.ask: In your own words: what is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
points: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after aggregates are computed
explain.model: `WHERE` is applied to rows before they are grouped, so it cannot see aggregate results. `HAVING` runs after `GROUP BY` and can filter on `COUNT`, `SUM` and friends.

concepts.title: Joins: combining tables
concepts.lede: Data lives in separate tables linked by keys. A join lines rows up by a matching column, and the join type decides what happens to rows without a partner.

data.title: See how each join treats unmatched rows

blocks.x:
SELECT t.id, c.name
FROM tickets AS t
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = t.customer_id;           -- INNER JOIN

SELECT c.name, COUNT(t.id) AS n
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN tickets AS t ON t.customer_id = c.id          -- keep customers with no tickets
GROUP BY c.id;

x: `INNER JOIN` (just `JOIN`) keeps only matching rows.
`LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row; missing partners become NULL.
Short aliases (`AS t`, `AS c`) keep queries readable.

blocks.x: To find rows **without** a partner (customers with no tickets): `LEFT JOIN`, then `WHERE t.id IS NULL`.

blocks.q: Which join keeps customers who have no tickets?
blocks.why: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table on its left, here `customers`.

exercises.prompt: Show each ticket's `id` together with the customer's `name`. Tickets without a customer can be left out.
hints: Two tables are needed.
Match `tickets.customer_id` with `customers.id`.
`FROM tickets t JOIN customers c ON c.id = t.customer_id`
exercises.solution: SELECT t.id, c.name FROM tickets t JOIN customers c ON c.id = t.customer_id

exercises.prompt: List **every** customer's `name` with their number of tickets as `n`, including customers with zero tickets.
hints: Customers with no tickets must survive the join.
Use `LEFT JOIN` from customers.
`COUNT(t.id)` counts only real tickets, so it gives 0 for no match.
exercises.solution: SELECT c.name, COUNT(t.id) AS n FROM customers c LEFT JOIN tickets t ON t.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id

exercises.prompt: Which customers have never opened a ticket? Show their `name`.
hints: Start from a LEFT JOIN.
A customer with no tickets gets NULLs on the ticket side.
`WHERE t.id IS NULL`

explain.ask: In your own words: why does `t.id IS NULL` find customers with no tickets?
points: LEFT JOIN fills the ticket columns with NULL when nothing matches
A real ticket always has a non-NULL id
explain.model: A left join keeps every customer. If none of their tickets match, all ticket columns come back as NULL. A real ticket has a non-null `id`, so `IS NULL` isolates the unmatched customers.

exercises.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN tickets t ON t.customer_id = c.id WHERE t.id IS NULL

concepts.title: Changing data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
concepts.lede: Besides reading, SQL writes. The golden rule: always check your `WHERE` before you run an `UPDATE` or `DELETE`.

blocks.x: `UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed'` **without** `WHERE` changes every row. Run the same condition as a `SELECT` first to see what will be touched.

x: Constraints such as `PRIMARY KEY`, `NOT NULL` and `UNIQUE` make the database reject bad data.
A **transaction** (`BEGIN` ... `COMMIT`) makes several changes succeed or fail together.
In these exercises changes affect a throwaway copy of the data. A check query then reads the result.

blocks.q: What happens with `DELETE FROM tickets;` (no `WHERE`)?
blocks.why: All rows go. The table itself stays.

exercises.prompt: Add a new customer: id `11`, name `Kai Nowak`, plan `pro`, country `PL`.
hints: Name the table and the columns.
Then `VALUES (...)` in the same order.
`INSERT INTO customers (id, name, plan, country) VALUES (11, 'Kai Nowak', 'pro', 'PL');`
exercises.solution: INSERT INTO customers (id, name, plan, country) VALUES (11, 'Kai Nowak', 'pro', 'PL')
exercises.after: SELECT id, name, plan, country FROM customers WHERE id = 11

exercises.prompt: Close ticket 4: set `status` to `closed` and `resolved_at` to `2026-09-19`.
hints: Only one ticket should change.
Set both columns separated by a comma.
`UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed', resolved_at = '2026-09-19' WHERE id = 4;`
exercises.solution: UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed', resolved_at = '2026-09-19' WHERE id = 4
exercises.after: SELECT id, status, resolved_at FROM tickets WHERE id = 4

exercises.prompt: Delete all tickets that are `closed` and have priority 1.
hints: Both conditions must hold.
A `DELETE` takes a `WHERE` just like a `SELECT`.
`DELETE FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed' AND priority = 1;`
exercises.solution: DELETE FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed' AND priority = 1

exercises.prompt: A teammate wants to close ticket 9 only, but this deletes the wrong data. Which line is the problem?
hints: Read what the statement actually targets.
Which rows will it change?
There is no `WHERE`, so every ticket changes.

why: `LIMIT` is not allowed in a standard `UPDATE` and does not say which row.
`INSERT` adds rows; it cannot change existing ones.

concepts.title: Subqueries
concepts.lede: A query can sit inside another. A subquery computes a value or a list of values that the outer query then uses.

x: A subquery in parentheses can return **one value**, **a column** (for `IN`) or **a table** (in `FROM`).
A **correlated** subquery refers to the outer row (`c.id` above) and is re-evaluated per row.
`EXISTS` stops at the first match, so it is often faster than `IN` for big tables.

blocks.x: `x NOT IN (subquery)` returns **no rows at all** if the subquery produces even one `NULL`. Prefer `NOT EXISTS`.

blocks.q: Which keyword asks whether a subquery returns at least one row?
blocks.why: `EXISTS (subquery)` is true when the subquery finds a row.

exercises.prompt: Show the `id` and `words` of every ticket longer than the average ticket.
hints: First you need the average length as a single number.
Put that query in parentheses inside the `WHERE`.
`WHERE words > (SELECT AVG(words) FROM tickets)`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, words FROM tickets WHERE words > (SELECT AVG(words) FROM tickets)

exercises.prompt: Show the `name` of every customer who has at least one **open** ticket.
hints: Find the customer ids of open tickets first.
Then keep customers whose id is in that list.
`WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open')`
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open')

exercises.prompt: Using `NOT EXISTS`, show the `name` of customers who have never opened a ticket.
hints: The subquery must look at the current customer.
Compare `t.customer_id` with `c.id` inside it.
`WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tickets t WHERE t.customer_id = c.id)`
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tickets t WHERE t.customer_id = c.id)

exercises.prompt: `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM tickets);` What does it return here? (One ticket has no customer, so its `customer_id` is NULL.)
hints: `id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` can never be true.
Comparing with NULL gives unknown.
The `NULL` in the list poisons the whole test.

explain.ask: In your own words: why does the NULL break NOT IN?
points: NOT IN means not equal to any value in the list
Comparing with NULL is unknown, so the test is never true
explain.model: `id NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` expands to `id <> a AND id <> b AND id <> NULL`. The last part is unknown, so the whole condition can never be true.

exercises.why: `NOT IN` with a NULL in the list evaluates to unknown for every row, so nothing passes the filter. `NOT EXISTS` (or filtering the NULL out of the subquery) avoids it.

concepts.title: CTEs: WITH clauses
concepts.lede: A common table expression gives a subquery a name so the query reads top to bottom, one idea per step.

x: `WITH name AS (...)` defines a temporary table that exists only for this statement.
Chain several CTEs with commas. A later CTE can use an earlier one.
CTEs are for **readability**. The planner treats them much like subqueries.

blocks.x: Write complicated queries as a series of small named steps and test each step by selecting from it.

blocks.q: A CTE lives:
choices: For the one statement that defines it
blocks.why: It is a named subquery for a single statement.

exercises.prompt: Use a CTE named `open_t` holding the open tickets. Then count them per category: show `category` and `n`.
hints: Define the CTE first, then select from it.
Filter inside the CTE, group outside.
`WITH open_t AS (SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open') SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM open_t GROUP BY category`
exercises.solution: WITH open_t AS (SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open') SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n FROM open_t GROUP BY category

exercises.prompt: Show the `category` of every category whose average `words` is above the average of all tickets. Use two CTEs.
hints: One CTE for each category's average, one for the overall average.
The overall CTE has a single row, so you can join it to every category.
`FROM per_cat, overall WHERE per_cat.a > overall.a`
exercises.solution: WITH per_cat AS (SELECT category, AVG(words) AS a FROM tickets GROUP BY category), overall AS (SELECT AVG(words) AS a FROM tickets) SELECT per_cat.category FROM per_cat, overall WHERE per_cat.a > overall.a

exercises.prompt: Show the `name` and ticket count `n` of customers who have **more tickets than the average customer** (average over customers who have at least one ticket). Ignore tickets with no customer.
hints: Count tickets per customer id first.
Then compare each count to `(SELECT AVG(n) FROM per_c)`.
Join to `customers` at the end to get the names.
exercises.starter: -- count per customer in a CTE
exercises.solution: WITH per_c AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM tickets WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT c.name, p.n FROM per_c p JOIN customers c ON c.id = p.customer_id WHERE p.n > (SELECT AVG(n) FROM per_c)

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order to build a query that lists the categories having at least 3 open tickets.
hints: A `WITH` block must come before the main `SELECT`.
The CTE body is inside the brackets.
`HAVING` comes after `GROUP BY`.

concepts.title: CASE, COALESCE, NULLs and dates
concepts.lede: `CASE` is SQL's if/else. `COALESCE` replaces missing values. Both appear in nearly every real query.

x: `CASE` checks `WHEN` branches top to bottom and uses the first that is true.
`COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first value that is not NULL.
Aggregates such as `AVG` and `SUM` **ignore NULLs**. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULLs.
Anything + NULL is NULL. Any comparison with NULL is unknown.

blocks.x: Date functions differ between databases: `julianday`/`strftime` in SQLite, `date_trunc` and date subtraction in PostgreSQL. The ideas carry over; the function names do not.

blocks.q: What is `COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 3, 4)`?
blocks.why: It returns the first non-NULL argument.

exercises.prompt: Label each ticket by length: show `id` and `size`, where `size` is `short` (under 20 words), `medium` (under 100) or `long`.
hints: `CASE` goes in the select list.
Check the smallest range first.
`CASE WHEN words < 20 THEN 'short' WHEN words < 100 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'long' END AS size`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, CASE WHEN words < 20 THEN 'short' WHEN words < 100 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'long' END AS size FROM tickets

exercises.prompt: For resolved tickets show `id` and the whole number of days between `created_at` and `resolved_at`, named `days`. (In SQLite use `julianday(...)`.)
hints: Subtract the two day numbers.
Only tickets with a `resolved_at` qualify.
`CAST(julianday(resolved_at) - julianday(created_at) AS INTEGER) AS days`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, CAST(julianday(resolved_at) - julianday(created_at) AS INTEGER) AS days FROM tickets WHERE resolved_at IS NOT NULL

exercises.prompt: Show every ticket `id` and its agent's name as `agent`. Use `unassigned` when there is no agent.
hints: Unassigned tickets must not disappear.
A LEFT JOIN gives NULL when there is no agent.
`COALESCE(a.name, 'unassigned') AS agent`
exercises.solution: SELECT t.id, COALESCE(a.name, 'unassigned') AS agent FROM tickets t LEFT JOIN agents a ON a.id = t.agent_id

exercises.prompt: A column holds the values 2, NULL, 4. What does `AVG(col)` return?
hints: Do aggregates count the NULL?
`AVG` ignores NULLs: (2 + 4) / 2.
If NULL counted as 0 it would be 2, but it is skipped.

concepts.title: Set operations and self-joins
concepts.lede: Stack results with `UNION`, compare them with `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT`, or join a table to itself to compare its own rows.

blocks.x:
-- customers with BOTH an open and a closed ticket
SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open'
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed';

-- combos in open tickets that never appear in closed ones
SELECT category, priority FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open'
EXCEPT
SELECT category, priority FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed';

-- self-join: pairs of tickets from the same customer
SELECT a.id AS a_id, b.id AS b_id
FROM tickets a JOIN tickets b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id AND a.id < b.id;

x: `UNION` removes duplicates; `UNION ALL` keeps them and is faster.
Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types.
A self-join needs two **aliases** for the same table. `a.id < b.id` stops each pair appearing twice and a row pairing with itself.

blocks.q: Which keeps duplicate rows?
blocks.why: `UNION` de-duplicates; `UNION ALL` does not.

exercises.prompt: Show the `name` of customers who have both an open ticket and a closed ticket.
hints: You need the customers who appear in both groups.
Two `IN` tests joined with `AND` work, or `INTERSECT` on ids.
`WHERE id IN (open ids) AND id IN (closed ids)`
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open') AND id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed')

exercises.prompt: Which `category` and `priority` combinations occur in open tickets but never in closed tickets?
hints: Take the open combinations, then remove the closed ones.
`EXCEPT` subtracts the second result from the first.
`SELECT ... WHERE status = 'open' EXCEPT SELECT ... WHERE status = 'closed'`
exercises.solution: SELECT category, priority FROM tickets WHERE status = 'open' EXCEPT SELECT category, priority FROM tickets WHERE status = 'closed'

exercises.prompt: List every pair of tickets raised by the same customer. Show `a_id` and `b_id` with `a_id` smaller than `b_id`, so each pair appears once.
hints: Use the `tickets` table twice with different aliases.
Match on `customer_id`.
`a.id < b.id` removes duplicates.
exercises.solution: SELECT a.id AS a_id, b.id AS b_id FROM tickets a JOIN tickets b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id AND a.id < b.id

exercises.prompt: You combine two result sets that overlap and want to keep every row, including duplicates. Which should you use?
hints: One of them removes duplicates by sorting or hashing.
The other just appends.
`UNION ALL`.

concepts.title: Window functions: ranking and running totals
concepts.lede: A window function calculates across related rows **without collapsing them**. Unlike `GROUP BY`, every row stays in the result.

blocks.x: Switch the function and toggle the partition to see how rows are numbered and totalled.

SELECT id, category, words,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY words DESC) AS rn
FROM tickets;

SELECT id, SUM(words) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running FROM tickets;   -- running total

x: `OVER (...)` defines the window: `PARTITION BY` splits rows into groups, `ORDER BY` orders inside each group.
`ROW_NUMBER()` 1,2,3...; `RANK()` leaves gaps after ties; `DENSE_RANK()` does not.
A window function runs **after** `WHERE`, so you cannot filter on it directly. Wrap the query in a CTE and filter there.

blocks.x: For **top-N per group**, rank in a CTE and then keep `rn <= N` in the outer query. This is a classic interview question.

blocks.q: Three rows have scores 90, 90, 80 (high first). What does `RANK()` give?
blocks.why: Tied rows share rank 1, and the next rank skips to 3.

exercises.prompt: Number each ticket within its category from longest to shortest. Show `id`, `category` and the number as `rn`.
hints: The numbering restarts for every category.
`PARTITION BY category ORDER BY words DESC`
`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY words DESC) AS rn`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, category, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY words DESC) AS rn FROM tickets

exercises.prompt: Show each ticket `id` with the running total of `words` in `id` order, named `running`.
hints: A running total is a sum over a growing window.
Add `OVER (ORDER BY id)` after `SUM(words)`.
`SUM(words) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, SUM(words) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running FROM tickets

exercises.prompt: Show the **two longest tickets in each category**: `id`, `category`, `words`.
hints: You cannot filter on a window function in the same query.
Compute the row number in a CTE.
Then `WHERE rn <= 2` in the outer query.

explain.ask: In your own words: why do you need a CTE for top-N per group?
points: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE
So you must compute the rank first and filter on it in an outer query
explain.model: `WHERE` is applied before window functions run, so the rank does not exist yet at that point. Computing it in a CTE (or subquery) makes it an ordinary column the outer `WHERE` can use.

exercises.starter: -- rank in a CTE, filter outside
exercises.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT id, category, words, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY words DESC) AS rn FROM tickets) SELECT id, category, words FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 2

exercises.prompt: Scores 90, 90, 80 ordered high to low. What does `DENSE_RANK()` return?
hints: Tied rows share a rank.
`DENSE_RANK` never skips numbers.
The 80 gets rank 2.

concepts.title: Windows for monitoring: LAG, daily metrics and drift
concepts.lede: Window functions shine for time series: compare each day with the previous one, or compute a metric per day. This is the SQL behind ReviewRadar's monitoring.

blocks.x: The `predictions` table logs every model prediction with the true label once known. Open **Tables you can query** to see it.

-- accuracy per day
SELECT day,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS accuracy
FROM predictions
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day;

-- compare with the previous row
SELECT id, confidence, LAG(confidence) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_conf
FROM predictions;

x: `LAG(col)` is the value from the previous row, `LEAD(col)` from the next. The first row has `NULL`.
Averaging a 1/0 flag gives the fraction of rows where it is 1. That is how you compute accuracy in SQL.
Daily accuracy, confidence and class mix are the first things to chart when watching for **drift**.

blocks.x: In PostgreSQL you cannot average a boolean directly, so use `CASE WHEN ... THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END` as above. It works everywhere.

blocks.q: What does `LAG(x) OVER (ORDER BY day)` give for the very first day?
blocks.why: There is no previous row, so the result is NULL.

exercises.prompt: For each prediction show `id`, `confidence` and the previous row's confidence (ordered by `id`) as `prev_conf`.
hints: You need the value from the row before.
`LAG(confidence)` needs an `OVER (ORDER BY id)`.
`LAG(confidence) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_conf`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, confidence, LAG(confidence) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_conf FROM predictions

exercises.prompt: Compute the model's accuracy for each `day`: show `day` and `accuracy` (the fraction of rows where `pred_label` equals `true_label`, rounded to 2 decimals), in day order.
hints: Turn each row into 1 (correct) or 0 (wrong) with `CASE`.
The average of those flags is the accuracy.
`GROUP BY day ORDER BY day`
exercises.solution: SELECT day, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS accuracy FROM predictions GROUP BY day ORDER BY day

exercises.prompt: Compare the two model versions: show `model` and its `accuracy` rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: Reuse the accuracy expression.
Group by `model` instead of `day`.
`GROUP BY model`
exercises.solution: SELECT model, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS accuracy FROM predictions GROUP BY model

exercises.prompt: Drift check: for each `day` show `accuracy` (rounded to 2 decimals) and `change`, the difference from the previous day's accuracy (rounded to 2 decimals). Order by day.
hints: Build the daily accuracy first, in a CTE.
Then subtract `LAG(accuracy) OVER (ORDER BY day)`.
The first day has no previous day, so `change` is NULL.
exercises.starter: -- CTE for daily accuracy, then LAG
exercises.solution: WITH daily AS (SELECT day, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS accuracy FROM predictions GROUP BY day) SELECT day, accuracy, ROUND(accuracy - LAG(accuracy) OVER (ORDER BY day), 2) AS change FROM daily ORDER BY day

concepts.title: Schema design: keys, constraints and normalisation
concepts.lede: Good tables make bad data impossible. Keys identify rows, foreign keys link tables, and normalising stops the same fact living in two places.

x: **Primary key**: uniquely identifies a row. **Foreign key**: a column that must match a primary key elsewhere.
**Normalisation**: store each fact once. Keep the customer's name in `customers`, and refer to it by id from `tickets`.
Pick types deliberately: integers for ids and counts, `TEXT` for strings, a real date type for dates, `REAL`/`NUMERIC` for decimals.

blocks.x: Storing a customer's name in every ticket row means renaming a customer requires updating hundreds of rows, and missing one leaves the data inconsistent.

blocks.q: A foreign key guarantees that:
choices: The value matches an existing row in the referenced table
blocks.why: It protects the link between the tables.

exercises.prompt: Complete the table definition.
hints: The first makes each ticket id appear only once.
The second forbids a missing label.
`PRIMARY`, `NOT`, `REFERENCES`.

exercises.prompt: Create a table `reviews` with `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` and `score INTEGER NOT NULL`, then insert two rows: `(1, 5)` and `(2, 3)`.
hints: Two statements: one creates the table, one inserts.
Separate statements with semicolons.
`INSERT INTO reviews VALUES (1, 5);`
exercises.solution: CREATE TABLE reviews (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, score INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO reviews VALUES (1, 5); INSERT INTO reviews VALUES (2, 3)
exercises.after: SELECT id, score FROM reviews ORDER BY id

exercises.prompt: Why is storing `customer_name` in every row of `tickets` a design problem?
hints: Think about renaming one customer.
Which rows must change?
Repeated facts can disagree.
choices: The same fact is repeated, so updates can leave the data inconsistent
SQL does not allow text columns

concepts.title: Windows: moving averages, frames and buckets
concepts.lede: A window can be a sliding frame, a bucket or a running total. Frames give you moving averages, which smooth noisy daily metrics.

x: `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is a frame of exactly three rows. It decides which rows the function sees.
`OVER (PARTITION BY g)` with no `ORDER BY` computes over the whole group, like a group average attached to every row.
`NTILE(n)` splits rows into `n` equal buckets, `FIRST_VALUE` / `LAST_VALUE` read the edges of the frame.

blocks.x: With `ORDER BY` and no frame, the default is `RANGE ... CURRENT ROW`, which treats rows with the same sort value as one group. Two rows on the same day get the **same** running total. Write `ROWS` when you want row-by-row behaviour.

blocks.q: `AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` averages how many rows (once enough rows exist)?
blocks.why: The current row plus the two before it.

exercises.prompt: Daily accuracy and its 3-day moving average: show `day`, `accuracy` (daily, rounded to 2 decimals) and `moving` (the average of the daily accuracy over the current and two previous days, rounded to 2 decimals). Order by day.
hints: Compute one accuracy number per day first, in a CTE.
Then average it over a frame of three rows.
`AVG(acc) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
exercises.starter: -- CTE for daily accuracy, then a frame
exercises.solution: WITH daily AS (SELECT day, AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS acc FROM predictions GROUP BY day) SELECT day, ROUND(acc, 2) AS accuracy, ROUND(AVG(acc) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving FROM daily ORDER BY day

exercises.prompt: For each prediction show `id`, `confidence` and `below_day_avg`: 1 if its confidence is below the average confidence of its own `day`, otherwise 0.
hints: You need each day's average attached to every row.
A window with only `PARTITION BY` does that.
Compare with `confidence < AVG(confidence) OVER (PARTITION BY day)` inside a `CASE`.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, confidence, CASE WHEN confidence < AVG(confidence) OVER (PARTITION BY day) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS below_day_avg FROM predictions

exercises.prompt: Split all predictions into 4 confidence quartiles. Show `id`, `confidence` and `quartile` (1 is the lowest confidence). Order the rows by confidence and then `id` inside the window.
hints: `NTILE(n)` creates `n` equal buckets.
The window must be ordered by confidence, with `id` as the tie-breaker.
`NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY confidence, id) AS quartile`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, confidence, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY confidence, id) AS quartile FROM predictions

exercises.prompt: For every prediction show `id` and `first_of_day`: the confidence of the first prediction (lowest `id`) on the same `day`.
hints: Partition by day, order by id inside each day.
`FIRST_VALUE(col)` returns the value from the first row of the frame.
`FIRST_VALUE(confidence) OVER (PARTITION BY day ORDER BY id)`
exercises.solution: SELECT id, FIRST_VALUE(confidence) OVER (PARTITION BY day ORDER BY id) AS first_of_day FROM predictions

exercises.prompt: Two rows share the same `day`. What does `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY day)` return for them?
hints: Think about what "up to the current row" means when two rows tie.
The default frame groups equal sort values together.
Use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` for strict row-by-row totals.

explain.ask: In your own words: why do tied rows get the same running total?
points: The default frame is RANGE, which includes all rows with the same ORDER BY value
ROWS makes the frame count physical rows instead
explain.model: With `ORDER BY` and no frame clause, SQL uses `RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`. A range frame includes every peer, meaning every row with the same sort value, so both tied rows see the same set of rows and get the same total.

choices: The running total up to each row separately
The same running total for both (rows with an equal sort value are treated together)

concepts.title: Monitoring a model in SQL: calibration, drift and per-class metrics
concepts.lede: Accuracy alone hides problems. Check whether confidence means anything, whether the label mix is shifting, and which classes fail.

blocks.x: Three questions every deployed classifier needs answered, each one query on the `predictions` table:

x: **Calibration**: when the model says 90% confident, is it right about 90% of the time? Bucket by confidence and compare to accuracy.
**Drift**: did the mix of predicted labels change between model versions or over time?
**Per-class recall**: which categories does the model miss? A good overall number can hide a class that fails.

blocks.x:
-- calibration buckets
SELECT CASE WHEN confidence >= 0.9 THEN 'high'
            WHEN confidence >= 0.6 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'low' END AS bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS accuracy
FROM predictions GROUP BY bucket;

-- share of each predicted label within its model
SELECT model, pred_label,
       ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY model), 2) AS share
FROM predictions GROUP BY model, pred_label;
`SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY model)` is a window over an aggregate: first `GROUP BY` counts, then the window adds those counts up per model.

blocks.q: A model's confidence is 0.95 on predictions that are right only 60% of the time. It is:
blocks.why: High confidence with lower accuracy means overconfident.

exercises.prompt: Check calibration. Put each prediction in a `bucket`: `high` (confidence at least 0.9), `mid` (at least 0.6) or `low`. Show `bucket`, `n` (how many) and `accuracy` (share correct, rounded to 2 decimals).
hints: Build the bucket with `CASE`, then group by it.
Accuracy is the average of a 1/0 correctness flag.
`GROUP BY bucket`
exercises.solution: SELECT CASE WHEN confidence >= 0.9 THEN 'high' WHEN confidence >= 0.6 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'low' END AS bucket, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS accuracy FROM predictions GROUP BY bucket

exercises.prompt: Check label drift. For each model and predicted label show `model`, `pred_label` and `share`: the fraction of that model's predictions with that label, rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: Count rows per model and label first.
Divide each count by the model's total.
`SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY model)` is that total.
exercises.solution: SELECT model, pred_label, ROUND(1.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY model), 2) AS share FROM predictions GROUP BY model, pred_label

exercises.prompt: Per-class recall. For each `true_label` show `label`, `total`, `correct` (how many were predicted correctly) and `recall` (correct divided by total, rounded to 2 decimals).
hints: Group by the true label.
Count rows, and count the correct ones with `SUM(CASE ...)`.
Recall = correct / total.
exercises.solution: SELECT true_label AS label, COUNT(*) AS total, SUM(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS correct, ROUND(1.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS recall FROM predictions GROUP BY true_label

exercises.prompt: Which mistakes happen most? Among the wrong predictions only, show `true_label`, `pred_label` and `n`, most frequent first (break ties by `true_label`, then `pred_label`).
hints: Keep only rows where the prediction is wrong.
Group by the pair of labels.
`ORDER BY n DESC, true_label, pred_label`
exercises.solution: SELECT true_label, pred_label, COUNT(*) AS n FROM predictions WHERE pred_label <> true_label GROUP BY true_label, pred_label ORDER BY n DESC, true_label, pred_label

exercises.prompt: True labels for ReviewRadar's predictions arrive days later, once agents close tickets. Which signal can you watch **immediately** to catch a problem early?
hints: Which numbers need ground truth, and which do not?
Predicted labels and confidences exist the moment the model answers.
A sudden shift in either is an early warning.
exercises.why: Accuracy and recall need true labels. The label mix and confidence distribution are available instantly, so a sudden change is the earliest hint that inputs or the model have shifted.
choices: The distribution of predicted labels and the confidence scores

concepts.title: Indexes and reading query plans
concepts.lede: An index is a sorted lookup structure. It turns a scan of every row into a few steps, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.

x: Index the columns you filter, join and sort on, mainly foreign keys such as `customer_id`.
A **composite** index `(a, b)` helps queries on `a` or on `a` and `b`, but not on `b` alone (leftmost prefix rule).
Every index slows `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` and uses disk. Do not index everything.

blocks.x: The planner may ignore an index on a tiny table or a column where most rows match. Always read the plan instead of guessing.

blocks.q: Which plan line means the database used an index?
blocks.why: SCAN reads every row; SEARCH ... USING INDEX jumps straight to matches.

exercises.prompt: Create an index named `idx_tickets_customer` on the `customer_id` column of `tickets`.
hints: Name the index, then the table and column.
`CREATE INDEX <name> ON <table>(<column>)`
`CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_customer ON tickets(customer_id);`
exercises.solution: CREATE INDEX idx_tickets_customer ON tickets(customer_id)
exercises.after: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index' AND name = 'idx_tickets_customer'

exercises.prompt: There is a composite index on `tickets(customer_id, created_at)`. Which queries can use it efficiently? (Select all that apply.)
hints: An index is sorted by the first column, then the second within it.
You must be able to use the **leftmost** column.
Queries 1 and 3 start with `customer_id`.

explain.ask: In your own words: why can't a query on only `created_at` use that index well?
points: The index is sorted by customer_id first
Matching created_at values are scattered across the whole index
explain.model: The index is ordered by `customer_id` and only then by `created_at`. Rows with the same date are spread out through the index, so it cannot jump to them; it would have to scan everything.

exercises.prompt: What is the main cost of adding many indexes to a table?
hints: Think about what must happen on every `INSERT`.
Each index also has to be updated.
More structures to maintain.
choices: Writes become slower and storage grows

concepts.title: Slow-query patterns
concepts.lede: Most slow queries come from a handful of patterns. Spotting them is a core skill for anyone who owns a database behind an API.

blocks.x:
-- 1. A function on the column hides it from the index
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE LOWER(name) = 'ana ruiz';       -- cannot use an index on name
-- fix: store normalised data, or create an index ON customers(LOWER(name)) in PostgreSQL

-- 2. Leading wildcard
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'Ana%';    -- can use an index
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%Ruiz';   -- must scan everything

-- 3. N+1 queries: one query for tickets, then one per ticket for its customer.
--    Fix: one JOIN.

x: **SELECT \*** pulls columns you do not need and defeats covering indexes.
**OFFSET pagination** gets slower on later pages. Use keyset pagination: `WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`.
In PostgreSQL, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and shows real timings.

blocks.q: Which `LIKE` can use an ordinary index on `name`?
blocks.why: A fixed prefix lets the database jump into the sorted index.

exercises.prompt: This query is slow even though `customers.name` is indexed. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at what the `WHERE` does to the indexed column.
The index stores `name`, not `LOWER(name)`.
Wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index.

choices: Compare the raw column, or create an expression index on `LOWER(name)`

exercises.prompt: A page loads 50 tickets with one query, then runs 50 more queries to fetch each ticket's customer. What is this called and how do you fix it?
hints: One query plus N more queries.
Databases are good at combining tables.
A JOIN (or `IN`) fetches everything at once.
choices: N+1; fetch customers with a single JOIN

exercises.prompt: Ask PostgreSQL to run the query and report real timings.
hints: Plain `EXPLAIN` only estimates.
A keyword makes it execute the query as well.
`ANALYZE`
exercises.template: EXPLAIN ____ SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE customer_id = 3;

concepts.title: pgvector: similarity search in Postgres
concepts.lede: An embedding turns text into a list of numbers so that similar meanings sit close together. pgvector stores those vectors in Postgres and finds the nearest ones.

x: Smaller distance means more similar. Sort ascending and take `LIMIT k`.
Without an index this is an **exact** scan of every row. `HNSW` and `IVFFlat` indexes are **approximate**: much faster, with a small chance of missing the true nearest neighbour.
You can combine vector search with normal filters (`WHERE customer_id = 3`) and joins. That is the retrieval step of RAG.

blocks.x: Cosine distance is `1 - (a . b) / (|a| |b|)`. It ignores the length of the vectors and compares only direction. You can write the exact search yourself in a few lines, and the exercises do.

blocks.q: A vector index of type HNSW gives you:
blocks.why: It trades a little recall for a big speed-up.

exercises.prompt: Complete the vector search.
hints: The column type comes from the extension and takes the dimension in brackets.
For cosine distance the operator is a symbol with `=` in the middle.
`vector` and `<=>`.

exercises.prompt: Write `cosine_distance(a, b)` for two equal-length lists of numbers: `1 - dot(a, b) / (|a| * |b|)`.
hints: The dot product is the sum of pairwise products.
A vector's length is the square root of the sum of its squares.
`1 - dot / (na * nb)`

exercises.prompt: Write `nearest(query, items, k)` where `items` is a dict from id to vector. Return the ids of the `k` items closest to `query` by cosine distance, closest first. (This is what `ORDER BY embedding <=> query LIMIT k` does.)
hints: Compute a distance from the query to every item.
Sort the ids by that distance and slice the first `k`.
`sorted(items, key=lambda i: cosine_distance(query, items[i]))[:k]`
exercises.tests:
docs = {"refund": [1.0, 0.1], "login": [0.0, 1.0], "billing": [0.9, 0.3], "crash": [0.1, 0.9]}
t("nearest([1, 0], docs, 2)", ["refund", "billing"])
t("nearest([0, 1], docs, 1)", ["login"])
t("nearest([0.5, 0.5], docs, 4)[0] in ('billing', 'crash')", True)

concepts.title: Transactions, upserts and locking
concepts.lede: A transaction makes several changes succeed or fail together. Knowing isolation levels and locks separates "it works on my laptop" from "it works under load".

rows: all changes in a transaction happen, or none
concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work
you read another transaction's uncommitted change
you read a row twice and get different values because someone committed in between
a repeated query returns new rows that someone committed in between

x: Higher isolation levels prevent more anomalies but allow less concurrency. PostgreSQL's default is **read committed**.
A **deadlock** happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs. Always update rows in the same order.
Make writes **idempotent** with upserts so a retried request does not create duplicates. That matters for any API that may be called twice.

blocks.q: What does `ROLLBACK` do?
blocks.why: All changes in the open transaction are discarded.

exercises.prompt: Customer 3 already exists on the `enterprise` plan. Write **one statement** that inserts `(3, 'Chika Obi', 'pro', 'NG')` and, because id 3 already exists, updates the `plan` instead (an upsert).
hints: A normal `INSERT` would fail on the duplicate key.
Add `ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ...`.
`excluded.plan` is the value you tried to insert.
exercises.solution: INSERT INTO customers (id, name, plan, country) VALUES (3, 'Chika Obi', 'pro', 'NG') ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET plan = excluded.plan
exercises.after: SELECT id, name, plan FROM customers WHERE id = 3

exercises.prompt: Close tickets 4 and 5 together in one transaction: `BEGIN`, two updates setting `status` to `closed`, then `COMMIT`.
hints: Start with `BEGIN;`.
Two `UPDATE` statements, one per ticket.
Finish with `COMMIT;`.
exercises.solution: BEGIN; UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE id = 4; UPDATE tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE id = 5; COMMIT
exercises.after: SELECT id, status FROM tickets WHERE id IN (4, 5) ORDER BY id

exercises.prompt: Lock the row you are about to update so no other transaction changes it first (PostgreSQL).
hints: It is a two-word clause ending in `UPDATE`.
The first word is a preposition.
`FOR`
exercises.template: SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE id = 4 ____ UPDATE;

exercises.prompt: Transaction A reads ticket 4's status twice and gets `open` then `closed`, because transaction B committed in between. Which anomaly is this?
hints: B's change was committed, so it is not a dirty read.
The **same row** returned a different value.
A phantom is about new rows appearing, not changed values.

exercises.prompt: Two transactions each update tickets 4 and 5, but one goes 4 then 5 and the other 5 then 4. They sometimes freeze each other. What is the standard fix?
hints: Each holds one lock and waits for the other.
A consistent order breaks the cycle.
Databases also abort one transaction when they detect a deadlock, so code should retry.
choices: Always update rows in the same order in every transaction

concepts.title: Analytics patterns: shares, cohorts, latest-per-group and gaps
concepts.lede: A handful of query shapes answer most analytics questions. Learn them as patterns and you can adapt them to any table.

blocks.x:
-- share of total
SELECT category, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM tickets GROUP BY category;

-- latest row per group
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM tickets WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)
SELECT customer_id, id FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

-- gap to the previous event
SELECT id, julianday(created_at) - julianday(LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id)) AS gap_days
FROM tickets WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL;

x: **Share of total**: `SUM(...) OVER ()` with an empty window is the grand total.
**Latest per group**: rank with `ROW_NUMBER` descending and keep `rn = 1`.
**Cohort**: find each entity's first event with `MIN(date)`, then group by that date.
**Gaps**: `LAG` the previous event, subtract.

blocks.q: Which pattern keeps only the newest row for each customer?
choices: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)` and keep `rn = 1`
blocks.why: Rank rows inside each group, newest first, then keep the first.

exercises.prompt: For each ticket `category` show `pct`: its share of all tickets as a percentage with one decimal place.
hints: Count tickets per category.
Divide by the grand total, which a window with an empty `OVER ()` gives you.
`ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1)`
exercises.solution: SELECT category, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct FROM tickets GROUP BY category

exercises.prompt: A customer's cohort is the date of their first ticket. Show `first_day` and `new_customers`: how many customers had their first ticket on that date. Ignore tickets with no customer.
hints: Find each customer's first date in a CTE.
Then group those dates and count.
`GROUP BY first_day`
exercises.solution: WITH firsts AS (SELECT customer_id, MIN(created_at) AS first_day FROM tickets WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT first_day, COUNT(*) AS new_customers FROM firsts GROUP BY first_day

exercises.prompt: Show each customer's most recent ticket: `customer_id` and `id` (latest `created_at`, ties broken by the larger `id`). Ignore tickets with no customer.
hints: Rank each customer's tickets, newest first.
Then keep only rank 1.
You need the CTE because you cannot filter on a window function directly.
exercises.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT customer_id, id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn FROM tickets WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL) SELECT customer_id, id FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1

exercises.prompt: For each ticket with a customer, show `id` and `gap_days`: the whole number of days since that **same customer's** previous ticket (NULL for their first). Order the window by `created_at`, then `id`.
hints: `LAG(created_at)` with a partition by customer gives their previous date.
Subtract the day numbers with `julianday`.
Wrap it in `CAST(... AS INTEGER)`.
exercises.solution: SELECT id, CAST(julianday(created_at) - julianday(LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id)) AS INTEGER) AS gap_days FROM tickets WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` on `tickets`?
hints: Think of a customer with three tickets.
One counts rows, the other counts unique values.
NULL values are not counted by `COUNT(column)`.
choices: `COUNT(*)` counts rows, the other counts different customers (ignoring NULL)

concepts.title: Alerting queries for model monitoring
concepts.lede: A monitoring dashboard is a set of queries plus thresholds. The art is flagging real problems without waking people for noise.

blocks.x:
-- accuracy drops of more than 0.3 versus the previous day
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT day, AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS acc
  FROM predictions GROUP BY day)
SELECT day, ROUND(LAG(acc) OVER (ORDER BY day) - acc, 2) AS decline
FROM daily
WHERE LAG(acc) OVER (ORDER BY day) - acc > 0.3;     -- not allowed: window in WHERE!
That last query is wrong: window functions are not allowed in `WHERE`. Put the window in a CTE first, then filter in the outer query. This is the shape of every alerting query:

x: 1. A CTE computes the metric per time bucket.
2. A second step compares with the previous bucket or a baseline (`LAG`, rolling average).
3. The outer query filters by the threshold.

blocks.x: Compare against a **rolling baseline** rather than a fixed number when traffic is seasonal, and require the condition on two days in a row to avoid noisy alerts.

blocks.q: Why can't you write `WHERE LAG(x) OVER (...) > 5`?
choices: Window functions run after `WHERE`, so they do not exist yet at that point
blocks.why: Compute the window in a subquery or CTE, then filter on the result.

exercises.prompt: Find accuracy drops. Show `day` and `decline` (the previous day's accuracy minus this day's, rounded to 2 decimals) for days where the accuracy fell by **more than 0.3** compared with the previous day.
hints: Build daily accuracy, then use `LAG` in a second CTE.
Window functions cannot be filtered directly.
Filter `WHERE decline > 0.3` in the final query.
exercises.starter: -- daily CTE, LAG in a second CTE, filter outside
exercises.solution: WITH daily AS (SELECT day, AVG(CASE WHEN pred_label = true_label THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS acc FROM predictions GROUP BY day), d AS (SELECT day, LAG(acc) OVER (ORDER BY day) - acc AS decline FROM daily) SELECT day, ROUND(decline, 2) AS decline FROM d WHERE decline > 0.3

exercises.prompt: Low-confidence share. For each `day` show `low_share`: the fraction of that day's predictions with confidence below 0.6 (2 decimals). Keep only days where it is at least 0.5.
hints: The average of a 1/0 flag is the share.
Filter groups with `HAVING`.
Repeat the expression in `HAVING`, or use a CTE.
exercises.starter: -- AVG of a flag, then HAVING
exercises.solution: SELECT day, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN confidence < 0.6 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS low_share FROM predictions GROUP BY day HAVING AVG(CASE WHEN confidence < 0.6 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) >= 0.5

exercises.prompt: Rolling confidence per model. For each prediction show `id`, `model` and `rolling_conf`: the average confidence of the current and previous prediction **within the same model** (ordered by `id`), rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: Partition by model so versions do not mix.
A frame of the previous row and the current row.
`ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
exercises.starter: -- frame of 2 rows, partitioned by model
exercises.solution: SELECT id, model, ROUND(AVG(confidence) OVER (PARTITION BY model ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_conf FROM predictions

exercises.prompt: An alert fires every time daily accuracy drops below a fixed 0.8, but ticket volume is tiny on weekends and accuracy swings a lot. What improves it most?
hints: Fixed thresholds ignore normal variation.
Small samples are noisy.
Persistence and a baseline reduce false alarms.
choices: Use a rolling baseline and require the drop to persist (for example two days), possibly with a minimum sample size
